stories.title: 4.2-magnitude earthquake hits Uttarkashi, second in Uttarakhand in four days
stories.summary: Officials of the Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) said no damage had been reported so far

article_sentences: A 4.2 magnitude earthquake struck Uttarakhand's Uttarkashi district on Saturday night (October 10, 2026), sending strong tremors across the Uttarkashi town and the Yamunotri valley.
According to the National Centre for Seismology, the earthquake, measuring 4.2, struck at 8.07 p.m., with its epicentre located two km northwest of Uttarkashi at a depth of 11 km.
Purushottam Uniyal, a priest from Kharsali village, the winter seat of Yamunotri, said the tremors were strong enough to cause televisions inside homes to shake.
The sudden and intense tremors triggered panic, prompting people to rush outdoors, he said.
Saturday's earthquake was the second tremor measuring above 4.0 on to hit Uttarakhand in four days.
A 4.9-magnitude earthquake had struck Chamoli district on October 6.
Officials of the Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) said no damage had been reported so far.

stories.headline: Saudi authorities say attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300
stories.title: Saudi authorities say attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300
stories.summary: Cairo, Oct 11: Saudi authorities say an attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more. According to a statement by Saudi authorities, the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, and one each from Palestine, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. It said some of those injured were in critical condition. The international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, was attacked again Saturday as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen. The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. On Saturday, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights and many people were wounded, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media. “We may. We're going to look at it,” Trump said of intervening. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly.” The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. Riyadh airport operations have been suspended Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended and the extent of injuries and damage was being assessed. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday. Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships. Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that. Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Officials have said US assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis. On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.” Flight disruptions are growing The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations. At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.” The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.

stories.headline: The legacy of a studio that captured a century in image
stories.title: The legacy of a studio that captured a century in image
stories.summary: “I recall feeling a profound sense of anticipation when I captured the quintessential aerial shot at a Reliance refinery nearly a decade ago. In my quest for the perfect photograph, I climbed a water tank, captured the image and felt a deep sense of satisfaction. I was unaware that the endeavour would turn me into a target for a swarm of bees. As I turned to climb down the tank, a swarm—or, more precisely, a storm—of bees enveloped me. I tried to flee, but all I received in return were more stings.” As Mr. Pavan Mehta showcases his remarkable collection of 900 cameras—ranging from a Yashica from the 1960s to a Rolleiflex dating back to 1905—he recounts the above incident as one of the defining moments of his photographic journey. He follows it with another story, equally compelling but deeply personal that traces the history of his family's enduring relationship with photography. Mehtas at the Maharaja’s Service Amarnath Mehta, a young man from Gurdaspur, travelled to Dalhousie, where a member of the military introduced him to the intricate craft of photography. In 1915, he began documenting Srinagar, establishing his studio on a houseboat on the Jhelum. As the studio expanded, it went on to preserve countless moments from Gulmarg and Pahalgam in Kashmir, extending its reach to Rawalpindi and Murree, now in Pakistan. Before Partition, the Mehtas held the prestigious position of official photographers to Maharaja Hari Singh, the last reigning Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir. In the early 1940s, amid the upheaval of the Second World War, authorities in Srinagar restricted the sale of photographic film to one roll per person to curb hoarding and the black market that often accompanies scarcity. A historical photograph of Europeans queuing for film remains preserved in the studio's collection. Following India's independence, Amarnath established a studio in Connaught Place in 1948, while the studio in Pakistan was eventually closed. Mr. Mehta recalls an era when family photography was a ritual woven into the fabric of everyday life—from celebrations to moments of grief. Around Diwali, families would gather to have their photographs taken and framed. Newly married couples would arrive in their finest attire, with women dressed in traditional ensembles and men in formal suits. Those who believed they had little time left would often choose to have their portraits taken, while relatives sometimes hurried to capture the final moments of a loved one's life in the hope of preserving the memory forever. With the arrival of smartphones, however, such practices have largely faded into the past. The Challenges of Smartphones and AI Although digital photography has made image-making more accessible than ever, it has also created a new challenge: preservation. While photographic negatives can survive for centuries under the right conditions, the long-term storage and organisation of millions of digital images present a different set of problems. Mr. Mehta emphasises the need for systematic cataloguing to ensure that these visual records are not lost in the digital age. For him, adapting to technological change is essential to survival. The studio has responded by publishing books and expanding into corporate, wedding, fashion and event photography, as well as food photography—areas that have helped make the business both commercially viable and sustainable. The studio's official Instagram account also carries short explainer reels featuring Mr. Arjun Mahatta, Pavan Mehta's son, who introduces viewers to a selection of vintage cameras. The initiative seeks to keep alive the enduring legacy of film photography at a time when digital technology dominates image-making. Photography as a profession, Mr. Mehta observes, is intensely competitive. Simply holding a camera, he argues, does not make one a photographer. A fundamental understanding of photography, acquired through study and practice, is essential to mastering the craft. Equally challenging is the task of developing a distinct photographic identity, particularly in an era increasingly shaped by AI-generated imagery. For aspiring photographers, Mr. Mehta offers a simple principle: “Before you shoot, see. Prior to engaging the shutter, it is essential to meticulously contemplate your composition. You observe, you anticipate, and you click.” In his view, patience, composition and an element of chance must come together to produce a photograph that approaches perfection. Asked to define photography in a single term, Mr. Pavan Mehta describes it as “art cultivated by curiosity” and a discipline in itself. “It is, quite literally, the act of creating imagery through the manipulation of light,” he says. “To achieve this, it is essential to comprehend the nature of light itself.” Drawing on Walter Benjamin's influential essay Little History of Photography, one can view photographs as visual records of existence—fragments of time preserved for future generations. It is precisely this quality that makes photographs valuable tools for remembering and interpreting history. Picturing a Century Pavan Mehta's book, Picturing a Century (1915–2015), offers a compelling illustration of this idea. The book chronicles a century of the Mahatta family's photographic journey alongside the social and political transformations of the country. Mr. Mehta points out that the family did not operate as an extension of any political party, yet its cameras documented pivotal moments in India's history, including the Kargil War and the funeral procession of Jawaharlal Nehru. Through their lenses, the photographers became observers—and chroniclers—of events as they unfolded. The story of Mahatta began with formal studio portraits captured on fragile glass-plate negatives and has since travelled through successive technological revolutions—from hand-painted photographs and film to digital imaging, selfies and, eventually, artificial intelligence. The studio has continually adapted to technological change. In 1954, it began hand-painting black-and-white photographs, carefully adding colour and detail by hand. It later became India's first authorised distributor of Kodak products. When photography moved from analogue to digital, Mahatta once again adapted, embracing India's first digital imaging system. Today, Mahatta & Co. operates from M-Block in Connaught Place, in a building leased from the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC). The family has operated its studio from the premises for generations. LIC, however, maintains that the studio is an “unauthorised occupant.” The Mahatta family disputes the claim, pointing to its longstanding presence in the building. Pavan Mahatta says the family occupied the premises even before LIC came into existence. He fears that forcing the studio to leave would mean Delhi losing an important part of its photographic heritage. The irony is difficult to miss. In the 1980s, Mahatta & Co. photographed the construction of the LIC building, designed by renowned Indian architect Charles Correa. Decades later, the studio finds itself on the other side of a dispute concerning the very premises from which it documented the city's transformation. The premises represent far more than a commercial establishment. They embody generations of the Mahatta family's photographic history in Delhi. For a studio that has spent more than a century documenting the lives, celebrations, tragedies and transformations of others, the present moment offers an unexpected turn: Mahatta & Co. has itself become part of the story it has spent generations recording. Syeda Shua Zaidi and Sadiya Tahseen are pursuing master in Convergent Journalism from AJK Mass Communication Research Centre, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi.

stories.headline: Chief Justice calls for greater representation of women in legal profession
stories.title: Chief Justice calls for greater representation of women in legal profession
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, on Saturday called for greater participation of women in the legal profession and urged judicial institutions to embrace technology to meet changing societal expectations. Addressing a felicitation programme organised by the Kashmir Advocates Association at the District Court Complex in Srinagar, the Chief Justice said encouraging women advocates and ensuring their active participation in the legal fraternity was essential for its progress. His remarks came as the Association announced that it had agreed in principle to induct five women lawyers into its Executive Committee, with the decision to be formalised shortly. Welcoming the move, Justice Bhati recalled the pioneering contribution of Cornelia Sorabji and stressed the importance of creating opportunities for women lawyers to assume greater responsibilities within the profession. Drawing upon his experience as a practising lawyer, the Chief Justice said the legal fraternity must remain responsive to changing societal expectations and technological advancements. He cautioned that institutions failing to adapt to emerging technologies risked being left behind. Describing lawyers as important custodians of constitutional rights and access to justice, Justice Bhati emphasised the need for cooperation between the Bench and the Bar to strengthen the justice delivery system. Earlier, interacting with judicial officers at the District Court Complex, the Chief Justice urged them to discharge their responsibilities fearlessly, compassionately and with an unwavering commitment to the rule of law. He said the judiciary had a crucial responsibility to safeguard citizens' rights, ensure access to justice and maintain public confidence in judicial institutions. Justice Bhati stressed that collective responsibility, mutual trust and institutional harmony were essential for the effective functioning of courts. He encouraged judicial officers to work collaboratively, maintain the highest standards of judicial conduct and create a peaceful and conducive working environment. Expressing satisfaction with the professional competence and dedication of judicial officers serving in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, the Chief Justice also highlighted the importance of continuous learning and guidance from senior judicial officers. Principal District and Sessions Judge Srinagar Naseer Ahmad Dar welcomed the Chief Justice and reaffirmed the district judiciary's commitment to quality adjudication, timely disposal of cases and reduction of pendency. At the felicitation programme, Kashmir Advocates Association president Waseem Gul highlighted the role of district courts as the first accessible forum of justice for ordinary citizens. He emphasised the importance of constructive cooperation between the Bench and the Bar and sought the Chief Justice's guidance on improving court infrastructure and facilities for lawyers and litigants. Gul also called for strengthening legal aid services, promoting alternative dispute resolution mechanisms and introducing structured training programmes for young advocates. He assured the Association's cooperation in improving the administration of justice and welcomed the newly appointed Principal District and Sessions Judge Srinagar. The Chief Justice appreciated the Association's decision to include women lawyers in its executive body and reiterated the need for professional cooperation, technological adaptation and inclusive participation in the legal system. The interactions focused on strengthening judicial institutions, improving access to justice and preserving the dignity and independence of the judiciary.

stories.title: High Court extends OPS benefit to employees appointed against posts notified before Dec 24, 2009
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has extended the benefit of the Old Pension Scheme (OPS) to the District Judiciary employees appointed against the posts advertised or notified prior to December 24, 2009, but subsequently joined service under the New Pension Scheme (NPS). The District Judiciary employees appointed against the posts or vacancies advertised for recruitment prior to the issuance of SR0-400 dated December 24 2009, introducing the NPS, and are covered under the NPS upon joining service on or after January 1, 2010, shall be entitled to exercise a one-time option for coverage under the OPS, according to an order issued by Haq Nawaz Khan Principal Secretary to Chief Justice. The order issued in keeping with the direction of the Chief Justice underscores that the option shall be exercised by the concerned eligible District Judiciary employee within the stipulated period of three weeks, that is up to October 30, 2026 from its issuance date. The order further emphasises that the eligible employee shall exercise the option for coverage under the OPS by submitting the duly completed form along with the requisite supporting documents, to the concerned Drawing and Disbursing Officer (DDO)/ Presiding Officer. District Judiciary employees who are eligible to exercise the option, but do not exercise the same within the stipulated time, shall continue to be covered by the NPS. The order indicates that upon receipt of the option forms, along with the requisite supporting documents, from eligible employees, the concerned DDO/Presiding Officer shall verify and certify the forms, prepare a list of employees who have exercised the option, and forward these to the Chief Justice Secretariat through the concerned Principal District and Sessions Judge, on or before November 12, 2026. The Chief Administrative Officer/Accounts Officer/S.O. (Administration), as the case may be, shall also prepare a consolidated list of eligible employees of the district who have exercised the option and forward the same to this Secretariat for cross-verification, it says. stories.headline: PDP: The “cry baby” of Kashmir Politics
stories.title: PDP: The “cry baby” of Kashmir Politics
stories.summary: The Peoples Democratic Party entered the political landscape of Jammu and Kashmir with the promise of providing an alternative political narrative. It projected itself as a party capable of challenging the traditional dominance of the National Conference and claimed to represent a softer, more responsive and people-oriented politics. Over the years, however, the PDP has increasingly transformed itself from a party seeking to shape political events into one perpetually complaining about them. Its political vocabulary today appears dominated by grievance, victimhood and accusations against almost every other political force. In that sense, the PDP increasingly resembles the “cry baby” of Kashmir politics—a party that finds reasons to complain about developments but struggles to offer a convincing political roadmap of its own. The PDP was created in 1999 under the leadership of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed and quickly occupied an important space in Kashmir politics. It challenged the National Conference at a time when the latter had long dominated the Valley's electoral landscape. Its promise of a “healing touch” appealed to sections of society looking for an alternative. After the 2002 Assembly elections, the PDP became part of the coalition government with Congress, and Mufti Mohammad Sayeed became Chief Minister under a rotational arrangement. The party had arrived as a serious political force. The difficulty for the PDP has been reconciling its rhetoric with its record in government. While in opposition, it frequently adopted an aggressive posture against those exercising power. Once in government, however, it was itself required to function within the same constitutional and administrative system it had criticised. This contradiction became particularly visible after the 2014 Assembly elections. The PDP had fought the 2014 election largely by presenting itself as a political barrier against the BJP's expansion into Jammu and Kashmir. Yet, after the election produced a fractured mandate, the PDP entered into an alliance with the BJP and formed the government. The alliance may have been justified at the time as an attempt to reconcile the electoral mandates of Jammu and Kashmir, but politically it exposed the enormous distance between the PDP's electoral rhetoric and its willingness to exercise power with the very party it had opposed. The BJP's ideological position was hardly a secret. Its views on Article 370, nationalism and the constitutional integration of Jammu and Kashmir had been publicly articulated for decades. The PDP nevertheless chose to share governmental responsibility with it. That historical fact makes some of the PDP's later political rhetoric difficult to separate from its own record. The death of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed in January 2016 was a turning point. Mehbooba Mufti eventually became Chief Minister and inherited not only the government but also the contradictions of the coalition. The unrest following the killing of Hizbul Mujahideen commander Burhan Wani in July 2016 created one of the most difficult periods of her tenure. As Chief Minister, Mehbooba Mufti had responsibility for maintaining law and order and defending governmental action. Her language as head of government was naturally very different from the language the PDP would subsequently employ from opposition. That contrast illustrates the central problem confronting the party. When exercising power, it has defended the compulsions of governance; when out of power, it frequently portrays similar governmental compulsions as evidence of injustice. A political party is entitled to change its position when circumstances change, but repeated shifts inevitably invite questions about consistency. The collapse of the PDP-BJP coalition in 2018 pushed the PDP into a political crisis from which it has struggled to recover fully. The constitutional changes of August 5, 2019 fundamentally altered Jammu and Kashmir's political environment. Article 370 was rendered inoperative in its earlier form, Article 35A ceased to operate, and the former State was reorganised into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The PDP responded by placing these developments at the centre of its political narrative. Opposition to the August 2019 changes is a legitimate political position within democratic discourse, and the party is entitled to advocate its constitutional viewpoint. But a political organisation ultimately has to tell people not merely what it opposes but what it proposes to accomplish under existing circumstances. This is where the PDP's present difficulty becomes visible. Its politics increasingly appears centred around a catalogue of grievances—Article 370, detention of political leaders and other persons, relations with the Centre, security measures, administrative decisions, the functioning of the elected government and the political positions of rival parties. On almost every major issue, the PDP presents itself as the aggrieved party. When the Centre acts, PDP complains. When the National Conference acts, PDP complains. When political space shifts towards another party, PDP complains. When its leaders leave, the party portrays itself as the victim of circumstances. When other parties appropriate issues once identified with PDP, it again complains of political betrayal or inconsistency. Politics, however, cannot permanently operate on grievance. A political party has to create hope, provide solutions and persuade people that it possesses a credible programme for the future. The younger generation of Kashmir is increasingly concerned about employment, education, entrepreneurship, tourism, technology, infrastructure and opportunities in the wider Indian and global economy. Constitutional and political questions remain important, but they cannot be the sole content of politics indefinitely. The PDP also faces a fundamental contradiction in its relationship with the National Conference. For years, it sought to distinguish itself from the NC. The PDP offered “self-rule”; the NC traditionally advocated autonomy. The PDP claimed to represent a different political approach and repeatedly attacked the Abdullah-led party for its historical record. Yet today the political space separating the two parties has narrowed considerably on several major issues. Both criticise the constitutional changes of August 2019. Both speak about restoration of constitutional protections, though their formulations and political strategies differ. Both compete for substantially overlapping segments of the electorate in Kashmir. The result is an identity problem for the PDP. If it takes positions similar to the National Conference, voters may ask why they need the PDP when the NC possesses a larger organisation and a longer political history. If it moves further towards sharper rhetoric merely to distinguish itself, it risks restricting its ability to expand beyond a particular political constituency. This dilemma has contributed to the politics of constant complaint. Instead of defining an entirely new political agenda, PDP frequently reacts to what the NC, BJP or Central Government is doing. Reactive politics may keep a party visible in newspapers and television debates, but visibility is not the same thing as political revival. The 2024 Jammu and Kashmir Assembly election demonstrated the scale of the challenge. The National Conference emerged as the dominant force in the Valley, while the PDP's representation was sharply reduced compared with the position it once occupied. That electoral result cannot simply be explained away by circumstances. It represented a message from voters that the PDP needed serious political introspection. The party has nevertheless shown that it retains pockets of political relevance. Its later success in the Budgam Assembly by-election demonstrated that political space in Kashmir remains fluid and that no party can permanently take voters for granted. But an isolated electoral revival cannot substitute for rebuilding a broad political organisation and developing a coherent long-term programme. The PDP must also confront the consequences of its own political history. It cannot erase the years during which it exercised power. It cannot speak as though every controversial decision in Jammu and Kashmir was taken by somebody else. Governments headed by the PDP faced protests, security challenges, administrative controversies and difficult political decisions. Political accountability does not disappear merely because a party moves from treasury benches to opposition benches. That is precisely why perpetual victimhood becomes politically unconvincing. A mature political party accepts responsibility for its own record while criticising its opponents. It explains what it did right, acknowledges what went wrong and tells voters what it would do differently in the future. Constantly locating responsibility elsewhere may provide immediate political convenience, but it does not necessarily rebuild credibility. Kashmir itself is changing. A new generation has emerged that did not experience many of the political events which shaped the leadership of older parties in the same way. Its aspirations are increasingly connected with education, economic mobility, technology, entrepreneurship, employment and access to opportunities beyond Jammu and Kashmir. Any party seeking a durable future must speak to these aspirations. The PDP therefore faces a choice. It can continue to define itself principally through grievances—against New Delhi, against BJP, against NC, against administrative decisions and against changing political circumstances—or it can rediscover the reformist political energy with which it originally entered Kashmir politics. A party that once challenged the established political order cannot indefinitely survive by complaining that the political order has changed against it. The description of PDP as the “cry baby” of Kashmir politics is therefore not merely a rhetorical expression. It reflects a deeper political criticism: the transition of a once agenda-setting party into an increasingly reactive political organisation. Kashmir does not need political parties competing over who can articulate the greatest grievance. It needs political organisations capable of offering competing visions of development, governance, employment, peace and democratic participation. The PDP has every democratic right to oppose policies with which it disagrees. It has every right to campaign for its constitutional positions and criticise both the Government of India and the elected government in Jammu and Kashmir. But opposition acquires credibility when it is accompanied by an alternative. The real challenge before PDP is therefore not to prove that it has reasons to complain. Every opposition party can find reasons to complain. Its challenge is to prove that it still has something new to offer. Until it succeeds in doing so, the image of the PDP as the “cry baby of Kashmir politics” will remain a political criticism that the party will find increasingly difficult to answer. Advocate Sunil Sethi, Chief Spokesperson BJP J&K

article_sentences: A week after the Irani Cup defeat exposed the cracks in its armour, Jammu and Kashmir gets a chance to reset on familiar turf.
The defending champion begins its Ranji Trophy campaign against Madhya Pradesh at the Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium on Sunday, hoping to leave that disappointment behind and find its feet again.
India pacer Auqib Nabi’s availability offers a timely boost, although J&K has rested Umar Nazir, who claimed six wickets in the Irani Cup.
Nasir Lone and Sunil Kumar provide further pace options, while Umran Malik, despite being with the squad, has not been considered.
The bigger concern, however, is the batting.
J&K squandered a first-innings lead against Rest of India before collapsing in the second innings.
Shubham Khajuria, Qamran Iqbal, Abdul Samad and captain Paras Dogra will need to shoulder the responsibility if the host is to make its home advantage count.
Building partnerships and avoiding another collapse will be central to its plans.
Madhya Pradesh, meanwhile, has spent the past week in Srinagar acclimatising to the conditions and arrives without any injury concerns.
Led by Shubham Sharma, it will miss Rajat Patidar and Venkatesh Iyer but retains considerable batting depth through Yash Dubey, Harsh Gawli and Himanshu Mantri.
The bowling attack, spearheaded by the experienced Avesh Khan and featuring Kuldeep Sen, has the pace to trouble the hosts.
Saransh Jain and Kumar Kartikeya add experience to the spin department, giving MP a balanced attack.

stories.headline: Concrete swallows Kashmir’s floodplains as natural defences shrink
stories.title: Concrete swallows Kashmir’s floodplains as natural defences shrink
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: Kashmir’s natural flood defences are steadily coming under pressure as concrete spreads across the Jhelum floodplain, wetlands lose ground and settlements expand into landscapes that once helped absorb excess water. A scientific study of the Jhelum basin has quantified the scale of this transformation: built-up land within the river’s floodplain increased from 55.47 square kilometres in 1972 to 203.30 square kilometres in 2013 — nearly fourfold in 41 years. “The population living within the floodplain also rose from 11.29 lakh in 1981 to 30.21 lakh in 2011, while the length of metalled roads increased from approximately 745.64 kilometres in 1962 to 1,698.23 kilometres in 2016,” the study notes. The findings, published in a study examining the climatic, geomorphic and human-induced drivers of the devastating September 2014 floods, reveal how rapidly development has transformed the Valley’s flood-prone landscape. The expansion matters because floodplains are not simply vacant stretches of land beside rivers. They form part of a natural system that accommodates excess water, while wetlands and drainage channels help regulate its movement. Construction, paved surfaces and obstructions can reduce water absorption, increase runoff and expose more people and infrastructure to inundation. The study also found that the area of major wetlands larger than 25 hectares in the Jhelum basin declined from 288.96 square kilometres in 1972 to 266.45 square kilometres in 2013, a reduction of 22.51 square kilometres. Researchers reported that 20 wetlands in and around Srinagar had been converted into urban colonies over five decades. Speaking to Rising Kashmir, senior environmentalist and researcher Dr Tanvir Ahmad Khan said: “Kashmir is committing an ecological blunder by allowing concrete to swallow its floodplains, wetlands and natural drainage systems. These are not wastelands available for urban expansion; they are nature’s own defence mechanisms against flooding. Every encroached floodplain and every reclaimed wetland weakens the Valley’s ability to absorb excess water and increases the vulnerability of people and property.” He said that the devastating floods of 2014 should have served as a permanent warning. “Yet, unplanned construction, indiscriminate land-use changes and the shrinking of natural water-retention areas continue to undermine Kashmir’s ecological security. The most disturbing aspect is that development often proceeds at the cost of the very natural systems that protect human settlements,” Khan said. “The government cannot claim environmental responsibility while allowing ecological buffers to disappear. Flood management must begin with protecting floodplains, restoring wetlands, removing illegal encroachments through lawful processes, and enforcing scientifically informed land-use regulations.” Khan said concrete may generate immediate economic gains, but when it replaces nature’s defences, society ultimately pays the price. “Kashmir cannot afford another warning written in floodwater,” he said. “The tragedy is that we are destroying nature’s protective infrastructure and expecting engineering and environmental mitigation measures and interventions to compensate for its loss. Embankments and drainage channels cannot fully replace functioning floodplains and wetlands.” The environmentalist said that the most alarming concern is the lack of political will to protect Kashmir’s floodplains, with short-term development interests repeatedly taking precedence over long-term ecological security and public safety. Dr Touseef Ahmad Bhat, a Kashmir-based environmentalist and socio-environmental activist, has repeatedly highlighted the interconnected nature of the Valley’s ecosystems. “Entire Kashmir is a wetland,” Bhat said, stressing the ecological importance of the region’s natural water systems. He also identified urbanisation, pollution, encroachment, land-use change and climate change among the pressures affecting wetlands, warning of consequences for biodiversity, water quality and human health. The concern is supported by research linking urban expansion and wetland loss with greater flood vulnerability. A 2023 study examining surface runoff in the Kashmir Valley found that rainfall exceeding 500 millimetres in the catchments played a key role in flooding, with northern catchments generating approximately 59.6 per cent of total runoff. It also identified built-up areas near rivers and below 1,560 metres as being at high risk of inundation. The evidence underlines the need to examine climate and land-use changes together. Heavy rainfall can trigger flooding, but the condition of floodplains, river channels and drainage networks influences how water moves through settlements. The Jhelum’s flood-management system also depends on the Flood Spill Channel, which diverts excess water from the main river. Designed to carry 8,000 cusecs, the channel requires adequate maintenance and protection against obstructions to preserve its intended function. Satellite imagery of 63 sampled lakes showed that seven were no longer visible or had almost dried up. The audit also found that 2,528.10 kanals of Hokersar Lake had been encroached upon amid the absence of proper survey and demarcation.
